question: Koch isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis in 1882 and used his postulates to prove causation. Which postulate establishes that the isolated organism is sufficient to cause the disease?

answers.text: Postulate 3 — the pure-culture organism reproduces the disease in a susceptible host

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Postulate 3 is the key causality step: the isolated organism alone must produce the disease when inoculated into a healthy, susceptible host, ruling out coincidental association.

answers.text: Postulate 1 — the organism is found in all cases of the disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Postulate 1 establishes consistent association (the organism is always present in disease), but association alone does not prove causation — the organism could be an innocent bystander.

answers.text: Postulate 2 — the organism is isolated in pure culture from the diseased host

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Postulate 2 ensures you are working with a single species (pure culture), which is necessary for a clean experiment, but isolation alone does not prove the organism causes disease.

answers.text: Postulate 4 — the organism is re-isolated from the experimentally infected host

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Postulate 4 closes the evidential loop by confirming identity, but causation is already established in Postulate 3. Re-isolation verifies the same organism — not a contaminant — caused the experimental disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review Koch's postulates in sequence: association (1) → isolation (2) → causation (3) → confirmation (4). Postulate 3 is the one that proves the organism is sufficient to cause disease.
Postulate 3 is the critical test of sufficiency: the pure culture alone must reproduce the original disease. This distinguishes a true causal pathogen from a coincidental finding.
